definition: Truth said of a thing is its conformity to the intellect on which it depends in being, rather than its being believed or observed. In ST I q.16 a.1, a true artifact realizes the form conceived by its maker, and a true natural thing realizes its proper nature according to the divine intellect’s exemplar (a true stone has the nature proper to a stone). This truth is secondary to truth in intellect. ST I q.16 a.3 relates a thing’s intelligibility to the being it has: truth adds a relation to intellect to the account of being. This is the ontological sense used to interpret the quarta via’s verum, not sentence truth, confidence, or frequency of endorsement.
note: The declaration’s verum is still an abstract respect: this definition records its intended source reading, not a mechanically enforced conformity predicate. Aquinas’s divine-exemplar account is recorded in its theological context; it is not used as an extra premise proving God’s existence. The comparative interpretation is separately stated in DEF-ONTOLOGICAL-TRUTH-COMPARISON.
